summary: The paper introduces Hessian-Enhanced Token Attribution (HETA), a post-hoc attribution method for decoder-only autoregressive language models that combines attention-value semantic flow, second-order Hessian curvature via Hutchinson estimators, and KL-divergence feature ablation. While the goal of improving interpretability in decoder-only LMs is highly relevant, the submission suffers from critical mathematical errors in metric definitions, extreme numerical anomalies in benchmark results, missing baseline data, and unconvincing computational feasibility claims for large-scale models.
strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely problem in Explainable AI: providing faithful, target-conditioned token attributions for autoregressive decoder-only language models.
Conceptually synthesizes three complementary perspectives—structural attention flow, geometric curvature sensitivity, and information-theoretic output shifts—into a unified attribution framework.
Proposes a new curated benchmark dataset combining NarrativeQA and SciQ to evaluate evidence attribution precision under controlled context distractors.
Evaluates the framework across a range of model families and sizes, including GPT-J-6B, Phi-3-14B, and LLaMA-3.1-70B.

key_concerns.issue: Mathematical impossibility in the proposed Dependent Sentence Attribution (DSA) metric formulation relative to reported results. In Section 5, DSA is defined as the difference between normalized attribution masses assigned to SciQ vs NarrativeQA segments, where total attribution mass across the input sums to 1. By definition, DSA must lie strictly in the range [-1.0, 1.0]. However, Table 1 reports DSA values as high as 5.10 for HETA and >2.0 for several baselines, indicating a fundamental mathematical contradiction or invalid unstated metric scaling.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Re-derive and clarify the exact formula for DSA, resolve the normalization discrepancy so reported numbers strictly align with the theoretical bounds of the definition, and re-evaluate all baseline results.

key_concerns.issue: Anomalous and order-of-magnitude performance leaps in Soft-NC benchmark scores. In Table 3, HETA achieves Soft-NC scores of 10.3, 10.8, and 9.9 across benchmarks, whereas all nine competitive baselines score between -1.48 and 2.15. Such an extreme jump (>5x to 10x higher than any baseline) raises severe concerns regarding unnormalized outputs, evaluation script bugs, or cherry-picked perturbation settings.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide a rigorous analysis explaining why HETA exhibits a multi-fold jump on Soft-NC, release the exact evaluation code, and ensure perturbation ranges and logit transformations are identically normalized across all methods.

key_concerns.issue: Unrealistic compute claims and lack of efficiency reporting for second-order Hessian calculations on 70B models. Computing Hessian-vector products (HVPs) requires second-order autograd backpropagation passes per token. Running m HVPs and T forward passes for LLaMA-3.1-70B on 2,000 instances of length 2,048 on a single 80GB A100 GPU is computationally and memory-wise infeasible without substantial unmentioned approximations, yet no runtime memory numbers or hardware benchmarks are provided in the main text.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include explicit wall-clock time, GPU VRAM peak usage, and throughput comparisons in the main text for all models, detailing how second-order autograd was executed for 70B parameter models on a single GPU.

key_concerns.issue: Omission of key baseline data and internal text-table contradictions. ReAgent is highlighted in the text as the strongest baseline, yet its results are omitted from Table 3 for GPT-J-6B and Phi-3-14B. Furthermore, Section 5.3 states that ablations and stress tests were conducted using Phi-3-Medium on TellMeWhy, whereas Section 6 states that ablations were performed on GPT-J-6B across four datasets.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Populate all missing rows in Table 3 for ReAgent across all models, reconcile the contradictory statements regarding the ablation experimental setup between Section 5.3 and Section 6, and ensure consistency across text and tables.

key_concerns.issue: Theoretical normalization issues in Semantic Transition Influence (Equation 1) and zero-gating effects (Equation 5). In Equation 1, the inner product terms V_i W_O 1 are not guaranteed to be non-negative, which can result in negative normalization denominators Z or negative transition weights M_T[i], contradicting the claim that M_T is a non-negative simplex. Additionally, using M_T[i] as a multiplicative gate in Equation 5 hard-zeroes out valid Hessian and KL sensitivity signals if attention rollout yields zero.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Apply explicit non-negativity operations (e.g., L2 norm or ReLU) before normalizing M_T[i], and investigate an additive or smoothed gating formulation in Equation 5 so valid curvature/KL signals are not discarded.

questions_for_authors: How can the reported DSA scores in Table 1 reach 5.10 when DSA is explicitly defined as the difference between two normalized probability masses summing to 1.0?
Why is ReAgent missing from Table 3 for the GPT-J 6B and Phi-3-Medium evaluations, despite being described in the text as the primary competing baseline?
What was the exact VRAM peak usage and per-sequence wall-clock runtime when executing second-order Hessian-vector products for LLaMA-3.1 70B on a single 80GB A100 GPU?
Why does HETA exhibit a 5x–10x score increase on Soft-NC compared to all baselines across three separate benchmarks, and how were perturbation step sizes controlled across methods?
calibration_check: The paper overclaims performance leaps and practical viability, backed by mathematically impossible metric values and unverified hardware execution claims.

significance.justification: Evaluating feature attribution in decoder-only autoregressive LLMs is an important domain, but the utility of the proposed method is obscured by severe evaluation errors.

novelty.justification: Combining attention rollout, second-order Hessian curvature, and KL feature ablation is a logical extension, though individual components draw heavily from existing literature.

rigor.justification: The paper contains a critical mathematical contradiction in the DSA metric definition versus reported results, alongside ungrounded HVP scaling claims for 70B models.

statistical_soundness.justification: Claims of standard deviation bounds (<0.06 / 0.2) lack confidence intervals or significance testing, and key baseline rows are missing from primary result tables.

calibration_honesty.justification: The manuscript presents unplausible 10x performance jumps and claims efficient 70B model second-order gradient processing on a single A100 without supporting runtime data.

clarity.justification: The main text relies heavily on missing appendix material, contains mathematical notation flaws in equations, and exhibits direct contradictions between experimental setup sections.

structure_compliance.justification: The manuscript adheres to standard ICLR structure with required sections, though critical empirical data is deferred to non-existent appendices.

reproducibility.justification: Essential implementation details regarding low-rank Hessian estimation, windowing parameters, and metric computation scripts are omitted from the main text.

related_work.justification: Prior interpretability methods including ContextCite, ReAgent, TDD, and Integrated Gradients are adequately cited and positioned.

figure_quality.justification: Figure captions clearly describe the pipeline and ablation setups, but the underlying mathematical definitions referenced in the text contain severe errors.

breadth_generality.justification: While multiple models and datasets are tested, key baseline comparisons are omitted for smaller model evaluations in the primary benchmark table.

overall_recommendation.justification: Rejection is recommended due to fundamental mathematical definition errors, anomalous benchmark metrics, missing baseline data, and infeasible hardware claims.
